title: Is a partitioned student rental near a university a good first investment?
excerpt: A 23-year-old freelancer wants a RM590,000 subsale let room by room to students, then a home. Sean likes the 7% yield, warns about partitions and exit, and says buy a second investment before a home.

question.asker: From A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: A is 23, earns about RM20,000 a month freelancing and has RM200,000 saved. A plans to buy a RM590,000 subsale unit within walking distance of a university, already partitioned and let to students, expecting about RM3,500 a month in rent against a RM2,450 instalment plus about RM1,000 for maintenance, Wi-Fi and utilities. A also wants a RM500,000 to RM800,000 home in Ara Damansara or Kota Damansara within the same year.
question.text: Is the student unit a good investment, and is buying a second property for own use in the same year too fast?

answer.quote: I think you are on the right track, bro.
answer.summary: Yes: about RM42,000 a year in rent on RM590,000 is a 7.1% yield, well above fixed deposits and the loan rate. But budget about 18% of the price upfront, understand the partition and exit risks, and use the second 90% loan on another investment rather than a home while young and mobile.

reasons.title: The yield is unusually high
reasons.body: With loan rates around 3.85% to 4%, a yield of about 4% covers the interest and 5% is already good. Over 7% is usually only found near universities, in busy expatriate areas or in holiday spots, each with their own risks.

reasons.title: Partitions bring legal and insurance risk
reasons.body: Kuala Lumpur City Hall has moved to ban partitioned living rooms, and partitions built without approval can void the fire insurance. Rent that depends on them may not last.

reasons.title: Student units sell only to investors
reasons.body: Families rarely want to live among student tenants, so the buyer later is another investor who prices by rent. If rents rise, the value rises with them, but if a nearby campus moves, demand can go too.

reasons.title: A home can wait
reasons.body: At 23 and working freelance, renting in a cheaper suburb such as Cyberjaya keeps costs low and options open. With this income, a second investment can be financed without waiting for the first unit's rent records.

actions: Budget about 18% of the price for down payment, stamp duty and fees, about RM106,000 here, before any renovation.
Check whether the existing partitions were approved, and what rent the unit would earn without them.
Check that the university nearby is a main campus that is unlikely to move, not a branch run from shop lots.
Declare your full income for tax: it costs a little more but helps the bank approve larger loans.
Keep six months of expenses and insurance in place, and learn other assets with small regular amounts.
caveat: If you want to live in a property later, the 85% rule applies instead: rent should cover at least 85% of the instalment so you can rent it out when you move. Sean assumed the income is steady; freelance income that varies changes the picture.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #230. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in November 2023, when loan rates were about 3.85% to 4%.
